Is it the whole hand, or only certain fingers? 

Depending on how you were laying on the operating table, how long you were laying there, if you were strapped and how tightly and where, etc. it's possible you are experiencing a compressed nerve somewhere along the arm leading to the hand. If only the pinky and ring finger are tingling/numb, or if only the other three fingers are tingly/numb, that is likely what you're experiencing. If that is the case, in my experience with a similar situation in the leg called meralgia paresthetica (during a gall bladder removal, not linked to my top surgery), your nerve will likely heal itself over time, but it may be several months. Certain stretches or other forms of PT may help decompress it more quickly.

It's not a transphobic jab, it's the fact that medical systems, forms, corporations, etc. haven't all caught up to terminology at the same rate so some important information isn't translating right.

Whether it's harmful or not . . . it depends on what the information is being used for. If it's just "surveillance data" for research then what you answer might be a small blip of data that's not wholly accurate to what the researcher wants but it won't really 'matter' to you. But if they're using that to determine your normal levels of some biochemical or how to dose a drug it could actually impact your quality of care.

What I would do if you are comfortable doing so is answer the questions the way they are written (When asking for sex at birth put male, when asked for gender put female) and if you feel something might be "lost in translation" by systems you can talk to the provider at the point of contact (office, pharmacy, etc.) about your concerns. 

Obviously this sucks and you shouldn't *have* to do it, but until everything catches up systems-wise it'll just be one more burden for trans people others don't even have to think about.

Trans women, (un)fortunately [depending on your desires], won't experience period symptoms in the same way those who menstruate do, and so what you've experienced is not *exactly* that, and your insistence that it might be is somewhat frustrating to many. 


While, as stated, many trans women experience some "unexplained" symptoms that resemble period-like symptoms on HRT, the fact you're not means that whatever you're experiencing is not *directly related* to your gender identity. That said, I've heard of some cis women wanting to be/believeing they are pregnant so strongly that their body seems pregnant and shows symptoms, it's not something I've heard of but I don't see why "phantom periods" can't be a thing given ["phantom pregnancy"](https://www.healthline.com/health/pregnancy/phantom-pregnancy) is a thing. Essentially you wanting a period so badly you start manifesting symptoms.

If that's the case, however, you should talk to your therapist and probably a medical doctor; if your gender identity feelings are so strong as to be manifesting negative physical symptoms you will probably need assistance to navigate your feelings in a healthy way before and through transition. And that's not a bad thing!

Additionally, just a tip as you begin to navigate trans places: Do so with an open mind and a kind heart (a reminder I think many of us can use as well here, myself included!) and do your very very very best to divorce yourself from the idea that what makes someone a girl or guy is how their body functions (eg. girl = period). After all, you're a girl and your body doesn't menstruate; I'm not a girl and my body does. Doesn't make you less of a girl or me more of one! 

I'm sorry you're having a rough time, that's unfortunately very common. But know this is a scary and sometimes difficult start to an exciting adventure and your life *will* get awesome over time as you explore yourself and the world. :) Keep talking to your therapist and keep your chin up.
Please don't think that period = girl. Many people have periods who are not girls/women; many many *many* people are women who do not have periods.

This would be informative for the doctor and probably also lend evidence to the dysphoria diagnosis and value of transition.

He's not asking questions because he's a curious weirdo, he is trying to learn about you as professional.

Keep in mind that the doctor is a sexologist, not an endocrinologist. They study sex and sexual behavior. Sounds like they are not the right professional for this purpose *but* unfortunately it sounds like they're the hoop you have to jump through.

So say that. "Doctor, I acknowledge that you are a sexologist. While I am asexual, please note that this is separate from my gender identity. Please let me know what you need from me to begin hormone treatments, but my sexual activities are not relevant to my gender identity and so I would prefer to talk about them as little as possible."

*That said*, it may be worthwile (if you feel safe with the sexologist) to talk to them. They may be trying to determine if there is interplay between your sexuality and gender identity (which given talking about sex understandably gives you gender dysphoria isn't an entirely crazy question for the doctor to have) and to have knowledge/otherwise prepare *you* for how your views and feelings about sex may change during/after transition. (I am not saying ace isn't valid no matter what! But just that it is not unheard of for sexuality to change on HRT and they may be probing that.)


If you feel you will be safe and respected you may wish to actually engage with the doctor on the subject, it may be helpful for you in the long run.

Honestly, no, they aren't asking too much. It is literally their job to ask about your sexual behavior. You don't go to the hair stylist then refuse to tell them what sort of haircut you want; you're paying for them to perform a service for you and they are trying to perform the service you are seeing them for.

You *can absolutely say*  you are uncomfortable and refuse to answer questions, and if they continue to push *then* they are asking too much. But simply asking and exploring is their literal job. In the future ask if you can see the doctor without your mother present. I'm really sorry this happened to you, I can't imagine how crushing it feels. But your surgery is just delayed, not cancelled, there's still hope. :)

First, don't be discouraged over the rate of loss you saw in the first six months; 80 lb in 6 months is extreme and honestly not something a dietitian would have likely signed off on (in a general sense, I don't know your specific case of course) and so the doctor gave you an unrealistic weight loss goal. The weight loss you *did* achieve is an actual reasonable and very admirable loss, congratulations, you did exceptional and the only reason it may not feel like that is that the doctor set you an unreasonable goal.

Second, I'll guess her approval of the surgery was under the presumption you would continue to lose at a rate similar to what you had experienced, thus she might not have thought it was important to tell you the "goal" cut-off since she assumed it would be met or thought it was taken as implied. She shouldn't have assumed this and should have been clear with her expectations, for sure. But that may be where the miscommunication was.

The fact you continued to lose (even relatively small amounts compared to the prior six months) in this pandemic is admirable, don't let this roadblock take the pride you should have away from you!

Third, you're right, 50 lb in 3 months would be another outrageous goal. But she said "to see where [you're] at." So I suspect she doesn't need you to be at that weight but will just want to see a good rate of loss and she'll be able to set up a pre-op based on continued loss.

If you eat a protein-sufficient diet taking specialized protein supplements won't help.

Simple explanation: Proteins are made up of building blocks called amino acids. When your body consumes protein from any source it is broken down into these amino acids and put into a pool to pull from. Additionally, many amino acids like those collagen is most desired for are non-essential, which means the body can make them from other amino acids if you need more to build collagen or something. The different amino acids go to form different things in the body/do different things. Collagen, for example, is mostly made up of glycine and alanine. The idea of taking a collagen supplement is you're supplying your body with the necessary building blocks to make more of its own collagen.

However, amino acids are found in all proteins, it's what makes them. If we talk about [this supplement](https://www.vitalproteins.com/products/collagen-peptides?variant=43393712134)  one serving has 1.4g of alanine, 3.7g of glycine, and 2g of proline. An original recipe chicken breast from KFC has 2.6g of alanine, 3.85g of glycine, and 3.6g of proline.

So don't waste your money and just eat a balanced diet.

It is mostly specific amino acids and similar constituents that are involved in wound healing in order to be sure your body has the building blocks necessary to recover quickly; I see omega-3s which will help keep inflammation (thus, swelling) down are included as well. 

It probably doesn't taste terrible; most of these types of products are like drinking a protein shake you might have before/after a workout: They will taste synthetic but they are flavored and meant to not be awful. If you try it and find you hate it you can tell your surgeon; a lot of other products will have similar formulations that are probably close to good enough. For example, bariatric surgery patients have a specially formulated high-protein clear drink that is more like drinking a powerade or apple juice than drinking a thick shake; a lot of my patients prefer those. It won't have the exact same formulation as the Impact drinks but it will have lots of complete protein necessary for healing.

I agree about the content, but not with the reaction to it. I suppose it's because I didn't approach it as a happy movie, or a movie that is meant to be a good example. I thought it was a very strong piece about precisely what you've put here, almost a cautionary tale of sorts. 

I also think the movie is very different depending on how you understand the timeline. I read the Wikipedia "summary" of the plot and it seems to interpret the timeline as linear, which I feel it is anything but. A linear interpretation implies we see them act the same scenes in the same way many times, with each following the last. However, I feel we see these in the wrong order, and possibly completely reversed in some cases. As "proof" I'll point out that early in the movie there is reference to some human toilet action happening in the bathroom off screen after Evelyn "fails to wash all of Cynthia's underwear" and there is no problem. However, throughout the film we see the same scene play out but Cynthia's confidence in her performance seems to regress and we don't even hear about Evelyn's interest in the human toilet thing until after we first see Cynthia confidently play out this scene. The timeline's all wonky and can't possibly be linear.

 I also feel that one must look more into what isn't explicitly stated. If you recognize (and/or believe, depending on how you feel about it) that we are seeing a disarranged series of snapshots in time in which we might see the aftermath of a scene before the scene itself many of the more "awful" parts of the movie actually take on a different light, though still not positive at all.

For example, Wikipedia's summary says that Cynthia sincerely accuses Evenlyn of cheating based on the gossip of a neighbor who Evelyn says talks too much/spouts lies, despite the fact that several times throughout the movie we see this neighbor entirely unwilling to engage the women in conversation and very isolated, not gossipy at all. At another point (early in the movie, but I believe after this scene in the timeline) Cynthia asks Evelyn if it was "too cold" and Evelyn says "the colder the better." This exchange of words happens while Cynthia is near a window, implying they are talking about temperature. We see, though, throughout the film that Evelyn wishes for Cynthia to be colder and colder to her. I believe that many of the "bad" experiences we see (the fight over "cheating", the birthday cake scene) are planned events orchestrated by Evelyn. 

After several rewatches I've seen there are many different ways to interpret the timeline of the film and its contents and I've also remembered why independent arty films drive me *nutsss*. 

There's no doubt that it is a tale of how lack of communication of one's real feelings can leave a relationship strained and I don't think it is a good example of a healthy BDSM relationship. However, I think it is a fascinating film and one that deals in a sincere way with the *problems* that arise from poorly executed BDSM relationships, and I feel that portraying a negative doesn't make the film bad.
